name: Arm span to height ratio

card.summary: The ratio of fingertip-to-fingertip arm span to standing height (the ape index), used to describe body proportions and reach, which shape how shoulders, arms and frame read visually.
card.aka: Ape index, wingspan ratio, gorilla index

quick.overview:
The arm span to height ratio, usually called the ape index, divides the distance between the fingertips of outstretched arms by standing height. A value of 1.0 means the two are equal; above 1.0 means arms that are long for the person's height. It is a measurement of proportions rather than something that is treated.

People interested in appearance use it to understand their frame: longer arms relative to height are often described as adding reach, a wider-looking wingspan and a different balance of limb and torso length. Sports research has examined it most, especially in climbing, basketball and swimming, with mixed findings on how much it predicts performance.
quick.how: It is measured by standing against a wall with arms extended horizontally and recording fingertip-to-fingertip span, then comparing it with height, either as a ratio or as a difference in centimetres. Lifters and climbers use the result to think about which exercises, clothing fits and sports suit their proportions.
quick.risks: Measuring it carries no risk. Arm span is largely fixed in adults and cannot be trained. Unusually long limbs relative to height can occasionally accompany connective-tissue conditions, so a clinician is the appropriate person to ask about a strikingly high value alongside other symptoms.

lead: The arm span to height ratio, commonly called the ape index (also wingspan ratio or gorilla index), compares a person's fingertip-to-fingertip arm span with their standing height. It can be expressed as a ratio (span divided by height) or as a difference in length. An index of 1 means span equals height [1][10].

In looksmaxxing and fitness communities it is discussed as a proportion that affects how the frame looks and moves: longer arms relative to height are associated with greater reach and a wider-looking frame, while a negative index means a shorter span than height. Because it is set by skeletal growth, it is treated as a trait to understand and dress or train around rather than something to change.

Research on the ratio comes mainly from sport science, where it has been compared across climbers, basketball players and swimmers, and from anthropometry, where arm span has been used to estimate height when standing height cannot be measured [3][4][5][6][7].

chain: Learn whether limbs are long or short for the frame
Choose training, sports and fit that suit those proportions
angle.text: The ratio describes proportions rather than changing them. People use it to understand how their frame looks and moves, for example how sleeve length, shoulder width and lifting leverages relate to their build.

paras: Arm span is measured with both arms stretched out sideways, from the tip of one middle finger to the other. Dividing by height gives the ratio. Vitruvius described a well-proportioned man whose span equals his height, an idea illustrated in Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man, and later statistical work moved from such ideals toward measured averages [1][10].

Surveys of US Army men reported averages of roughly 1.03 to 1.04 [10]. Elite bouldering athletes in a 2025 study averaged around 1.06 according to a summary of the literature [1], and the NBA average is reported near 1.06 [10].

Climbers, swimmers, boxers and basketball players are the groups most often discussed. Longer arms are described as helping with reach, stroke length and striking distance, although published reviews describe findings as mixed and note that strength, technique and flexibility matter in their own right [1][2][10].

A 2023 systematic review of sport climbers compared body composition, anthropometrics including ape index, and strength measures between ability levels and non-climbers [2]. A 2025 study of male World Cup bouldering athletes found international-level climbers had lower body fat than national-level athletes and reported ape index among the measured proportions [3]. Other studies examined the physique and performance structure of competitive climbers [4][5]. Climbers such as Lynn Hill have succeeded with a negative index [10].

In clinical and field anthropometry, arm span serves as a proxy for height when someone cannot stand straight, for example older adults with spinal curvature or children. Published studies have derived such estimates for north Indian subjects, Malawian children and the Dhimal population of West Bengal [6][7][8].

Forum discussion treats a high ape index as a framing advantage for wingspan, shoulder-to-height presence and certain lifts, and a low one as an area to dress around. Tailoring sleeve length, jacket fit and choice of exercises are among the practical ways people respond to their proportions.

No trials have tested interventions to change the ratio. Observational studies have measured it in athletes and in population samples [2][3][8], and arm span has been validated as a height proxy in several populations [6][7][8].

timeline.event: Vitruvius describes arm span equal to height as an ideal proportion [10].
Study of elite male bouldering athletes reports ape index among measured proportions [3].
